The variable aperture lens on the new iPhone 18 Pro is nearly a full stop wider than the fixed aperture on its predecessor: jumping from f/1.78 on the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48 (remember: the smaller the number, the wider the aperture).

In theory, this should deliver slightly shallower depth of field, giving better separation between subject and background—though the difference is relatively modest. But there are actually four ways to achieve a shallow depth of field that have been available on iPhones for years…

Portrait Mode

The most obvious method is to use Portrait mode, which is literally designed to separate your subject clearly from the background.

It's a purely computational effect (aided by LiDAR on equipped models) that identifies the subject and then artificially blurs everything else. Early versions looked rough, but in recent years it has improved dramatically and produces excellent results.

Macro Photography

The second method is to use macro mode, which kicks in automatically when you get very close to your subject. Once activated, the iPhone switches to the ultra-wide lens, since it can focus at very short distances.

In this mode, only a range of a few centimetres will be sharp, with everything beyond growing progressively more blurred. As you can see in the example below, be prepared to spend a lot of time wiping and cleaning before shooting in this mode! A small yellow flower icon in the bottom-right corner of the frame indicates the mode is active.

Moving Close to the Subject

You can also use the standard lens and get a similar effect simply by moving very close to your subject. For example:

Just tap on whatever object or person you want to focus on before shooting.

Telephoto Lens

Another factor affecting depth of field is focal length. All else being equal, the longer the focal length, the shallower the depth of field, so using the telephoto lens on your iPhone can also produce a slightly blurred background.

Combine All Three

Using all three methods together yields the best results:

  • Select the telephoto lens
  • Keep your subject as far from the background as possible
  • Get as close to your subject as you can

This approach works best for photographing people, and it's even more effective on the iPhone 15 Pro and later thanks to their longer focal lengths.

Conclusion

The wider variable aperture lens is just one of many new camera features on the iPhone 18 Pro, and if photography is the feature you use most on your phone, upgrading is still worth considering. But if your goal is to achieve a blurred-background effect, there are other methods that can deliver the same result.
